description: An evergreen, glossy-leaved shrub 2-4 m tall bearing large showy funnel-shaped flowers, most commonly red, with a prominent protruding column of stamens fused around the style. Many garden colours exist.
cultural_significance: Red hibiscus is offered to Goddess Kali and Durga, and to Lord Ganesha, and is a symbol of devotion in Bengal. Used in Ayurvedic hair oils. Not a Vedic-era plant by name; prominent in later texts and tantric worship.
habitat: Warm tropical and subtropical regions; very commonly planted in gardens, hedges and temple precincts across India.

uses.title: Hair and scalp care
uses.detail: Flowers and leaves are ground into pastes or simmered in coconut oil, traditionally used to support hair growth and reduce dandruff.

uses.title: Menstrual conditions
uses.detail: Flowers are described in traditional use for heavy or irregular menstrual bleeding; use under guidance.

uses.title: Cooling flower tea
uses.detail: Petals are steeped in water as a cooling, slightly tart drink and used for coughs and sore throats.

uses.title: Blood pressure research
uses.detail: Studies mostly on Hibiscus sabdariffa (roselle), a different species, show BP effects; evidence for H. rosa-sinensis is preliminary.

preparations.name: Hair oil
preparations.method: Simmer fresh flowers and leaves in coconut oil on low heat until moisture evaporates; strain and cool.
preparations.note: External use for scalp; patch test first.

preparations.name: Flower paste (lepa)
preparations.method: Grind petals and leaves with water into a paste for hair or skin.

preparations.name: Hibiscus tea
preparations.method: Steep fresh or dried petals in hot water for 5-10 minutes; strain.

preparations.name: Flower sherbet
preparations.method: Boil petals with water, strain and sweeten for a cooling drink.

precautions: Traditionally avoided in pregnancy because root and flower have been described as having anti-fertility and uterine-stimulating effects. May lower blood pressure and blood sugar, so people on BP or diabetes medicines should consult a doctor. Do not confuse with Hibiscus sabdariffa (roselle); allergy to Malvaceae plants is possible.

cultivation.water: Regular; keep evenly moist but not waterlogged
cultivation.propagation: Stem cuttings or grafting; named varieties are cloned
cultivation.harvest: Flowers are picked fresh in the morning; blooms last a day

conservation_status: Not threatened; origin uncertain and widely cultivated.
fun_fact: Each hibiscus flower lasts only about a day, and the flower was historically used to polish shoes in some regions, giving it the name 'shoe flower'.

regions.name: Southern China
regions.note: Widely cultivated and used in traditional medicine
